title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
formal:
Determine the growth, up to universal multiplicative constants, of the optimal randomized competitive ratio for \(k\)-server on all finite metrics against an oblivious adversary. For each integer \(k\ge2\), define
\[R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where \(\mathcal R_k\) is the set of real \(r\ge1\) such that
\[\forall (X,d)\in\mathcal M_k\;\forall C_0\in X^k\;\exists\mathcal A\;\exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\;\forall\sigma\in X^{<\omega},\qquad
\mathbb E_U[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathcal A}(\sigma;C_0,U)]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite metric spaces with at least \(k+1\) points, and \(\mathcal A\) is an online randomized strategy as defined below. Give an unambiguous positive function \(h\) on the integers \(k\ge2\) and fixed real constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\) such that
\[a h(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le b h(k)\qquad\text{for all integers }k\ge2.\]
The requested precision is matching asymptotic bounds, including any logarithmic dependence.
definitions:
A metric on a finite set \(X\) is a finite-valued function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry and the triangle inequality. The number \(n=|X|\) is unbounded relative to \(k\). The strategy knows the full metric and initial configuration before any request. Distances may be arbitrary real numbers: no rational encoding, finite-precision cost or computability restriction is imposed on this information-theoretic question.

Exactly \(k\) identical servers serve the requests. For bookkeeping write a configuration as a tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in X^k\); repeated locations are allowed and the labels confer no different costs. A finite sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\) is revealed one request at a time. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay and this step costs zero. Otherwise the strategy chooses one server, moves it from its current position \(x_i\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_i,q_t)\). All other servers stay. The total cost is the sum over the \(T\) steps. This lazy convention has the same attainable competitive guarantees as the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances model. It is not a simultaneous maximum-movement objective.

An online strategy is a measurable rule whose move depends on the known metric, \(k,C_0\), the revealed request prefix, its past choices and its private randomness. One may model the randomness by a uniform seed \(U\in[0,1]\). It must make a legal move for every prefix and seed, and serve the current request before observing the next. No future request, request horizon, prediction or advice depending on the sequence is supplied. There is no time, space, number-of-random-bits or finite-program bound. The same seed law and nonanticipating rule serve all finite sequences on the chosen instance.

The adversary is oblivious: each sequence \(\sigma\) in the guarantee is fixed independently of \(U\). It may know the strategy and its distribution, but may not choose the next request from observed random moves. Expectation is over \(U\), for that fixed sequence. Every finite-sequence cost is bounded by \(T\) times the finite metric diameter, so the expectation is finite. The offline comparator starts at the identical tuple \(C_0\), knows all of \(\sigma\), and minimizes total movement under the same serving convention. This minimum exists because there are finitely many possible server choices for a finite sequence. The empty sequence has online and offline cost zero.

For fixed \(k,r\), the strategy and finite additive term \(\beta\) may depend on the metric and initial tuple, but neither may depend on the future sequence or its length. The ratio \(r\), and ultimately the comparison constants \(a,b\), cannot depend on \(n\), distances or initial placement. The same chosen strategy and \(\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all lengths and contents. Classical deterministic bounds imply \(1\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le2k-1\), so the infimum is a finite dimensionless number. No strategy attaining the infimum is presumed to exist.

An upper bound on this infimum need not give an algorithm attaining its endpoint: for every positive slack, strategies with ratios at most the proposed upper bound plus that slack suffice on every metric and initial placement. A lower bound must exclude every smaller universal ratio; for such a smaller ratio some metric and initial placement must defeat every eligible strategy and every fixed additive constant on a sequence independent of the realized seed. The unknown function \(h\) must specify the asymptotic scale, rather than merely rename the defining infimum.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, all distances between distinct points equal one, and the server positions represent pages held in a cache. General metrics give different costs for replacing one location by another. Randomization can protect an online strategy from a fixed request sequence, but the comparator sees the whole sequence and has the same number of servers.

The old randomized conjecture proposed an \(O(\log k)\) ratio on every metric. Bubeck, Coester and Rabani refute it with \((k+1)\)-point metrics requiring \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) randomized competitiveness. Their definition permits an arbitrary fixed additive constant and compares expected online cost to offline cost, matching the relevant convention here. The obstruction still leaves possible larger polylogarithmic ratios.

The \((k+1)\)-point special case has order \(\Theta(\log^2 k)\) through its connection with metrical service and task systems. This does not determine the card's function, which takes the worst case over every finite number of metric points. Allowing \(n\) much larger than \(k\) is an essential part of the remaining target.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 paper gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on hierarchically separated trees. These are a structured class of leaf metrics of weighted rooted trees whose edge scales decrease geometrically by a fixed factor along root-to-leaf paths. Theorem 1 also bounds the amount of randomness independently of request-sequence length. The geometry restriction matters to the competitive guarantee.

Their Corollary 2 gives \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\) competitiveness on arbitrary \(n\)-point metrics. This is a computational improvement, but the factor \(\log n\) cannot be hidden in a universal function of \(k\). The same paper explicitly states that even an \(o(k)\) ratio on arbitrary metrics remains open. Its separate advice-assisted consequence has additional future-dependent information and is not the oblivious randomized model here.

The classical deterministic \(2k-1\) guarantee is also a randomized upper bound, because a randomized strategy may ignore its coins. Together with the squared-logarithmic lower bound, it leaves a gap between \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) and \(O(k)\). The quantitative question is to determine the entire asymptotic scale within this gap, not just to improve one endpoint.

The September 2026 preprint by Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński claims that the deterministic work-function algorithm attains ratio \(k\) on every metric. If correct, it also gives \(R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le k\); it does not supply a randomized lower bound of \(k\), or improve the order \(O(k)\). Its theorem therefore does not settle this card's matching-asymptotics target. The new proof has not been independently certified in this review.

The weaker milestone formerly indexed as TCS-4983 asks whether there is a function \(r(k)\ge1\) with \(r(k)/k\to0\) such that, for every finite metric and initial placement, some randomized online strategy has competitive ratio at most \(r(k)\), allowing a fixed sequence-independent additive cost. In the present model this is equivalent to \(R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)/k\to0\). If the latter holds, the positive slack \(r(k)=R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)+1\) accommodates possible nonattainment of the defining infimum. Thus a determination of this card's asymptotic scale also captures the sublinear milestone. The same ICALP 2026 source explicitly poses it; its polynomial-time results do not impose an additional running-time requirement on that open question.

why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both displayed inequalities for some unambiguous \(h\) and universal \(a,b\). This is the retained constant-factor asymptotic-complexity target, not an additive numerical approximation requirement. Upper bounds must cover all finite metrics, all initial placements and all obliviously chosen finite request sequences with the permitted additive term. Lower bounds must cover every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics and cannot rely on an adversary observing its random outcomes. Respect possible nonattainment of the infimum. A one-sided improvement, a bound depending on \(|X|\), or a determination restricted to one metric family does not establish the full scale.

progress.text: The deterministic work-function algorithm achieves factor 2k minus 1, giving a linear-in-k upper bound also when randomness is allowed.
The Bubeck–Coester–Rabani preprint, published at STOC 2023, gives a squared-logarithmic randomized lower bound on suitable (k+1)-point metrics and refutes the old logarithmic conjecture.
Coester and Cosson give computationally efficient randomized algorithms while retaining a log n factor on arbitrary n-point metrics. Their paper distinguishes the remaining k-only question.
A new preprint claims deterministic factor k on all metrics. Even if correct, it leaves the randomized upper bound linear in k and does not close the asymptotic gap.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The final ICALP 2026 primary source retains the arbitrary-metric o(k) randomized question and gives a log n-dependent general guarantee; the 2023 lower bound is squared-logarithmic in k. The September deterministic factor-k claim, arXiv:2609.15979v1, would improve a constant in the available linear upper bound but does not determine the randomized asymptotic scale. No matching randomized resolution was located in the bounded search. The card remains source_open for its explicitly quantitative constant-factor target; the fresh deterministic proof is not independently certified here.

sentences: An online strategy moves k identical servers to serve requests in a finite metric space, paying total movement distance.
The adversary fixes the request sequence independently of the strategy’s private randomness.
The target is the universal optimal expected competitive ratio as a function of k, with matching upper and lower bounds up to constant factors.
The metric and initial placement may affect the strategy and fixed additive cost, but the multiplicative ratio cannot depend on the number of metric points.
The new deterministic factor-k claim leaves the randomized gap between squared-logarithmic and linear growth unresolved.

The earlier logarithmic conjecture is false; the weaker question of any fixed polylogarithmic bound is distinct from both that conjecture and the full quantitative target. The September deterministic conjecture claim does not replace this randomized question.
